entry.title: Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved
entry.content:
Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved

Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved

30 October 2026

Why do our grids show a brief spike in electricity demand every minute? A team led by Dirk Witthaut from Forschungszentrum Jülich has now demonstrated that this is due to regular power checks carried out by large-scale battery storage systems. These findings could help to make our electricity supply more robust, as the team reports in an article published in Nature Energy.

Tennet Germany, the largest transmission system operator in Germany, has observed over several years that the frequency in the European power grid dips briefly every 60 seconds. While these deviations were not critical to grid security, they were clearly measurable and unusually regular. The cause of this phenomenon was initially unclear.

A team from Jülich led by Dirk Witthaut, together with researchers from the University of Cologne and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, set out to investigate – and found the answer: the cause appears to be the many large-scale battery storage systems that check their state of charge every minute. This leads to measurable fluctuations in electricity consumption, which can contribute to turbine wear and tear, for example. The battery storage systems ensure an uninterrupted power supply, and their numbers have increased significantly worldwide in recent years. The researchers found that this was not a European phenomenon, but a global one.

Many devices, a common rhythm

“It really was years of detective work,” says Witthaut. The grid frequency pattern is shaped by many different factors. For example, it reveals the influence of electricity trading, with power stations being switched on and off abruptly, as well as the fluctuating feed-in from renewable energy sources, and various other disturbances.

Uns war schnell klar, dass es sich bei der Ursache um etwas handeln muss, das von der Uhr gesteuert wird

“It quickly became clear to us that the cause must be something controlled by the clock,” says Witthaut. There was no other way to explain the precise 60-second cycle. It was also clear that: “The observed effect can only be produced if many devices are consuming electricity at the same time.” A single consumer or generator could therefore be ruled out.

Measurements on campus provide the clue

But how do all these devices synchronize their consumption? The researchers finally found the crucial clues with the help of the Living Lab Energy Campus. This research infrastructure on the Jülich campus is primarily used to develop and test highly integrated energy supply systems. The team installed measuring points on end devices at a total of 80 locations – and sure enough, the same periodic pattern in electricity consumption was observed precisely at the locations where large-scale battery storage systems are designed to ensure an uninterrupted power supply. “We took a closer look at one of them and found a spike in electricity consumption at the start of every minute due to the power check,” explains Witthaut.

As there are no binding standards for such power checks, Witthaut suspects that most battery manufacturers assumed that a 60-second interval would be sensible. The start of every minute was simply chosen as the test time. “It is entirely possible, however, that battery storage systems are only part of the problem here,” says Witthaut. “It cannot be ruled out that other digitally controlled appliances – such as air-conditioning systems, heat pumps, washing machines, and dishwashers – may also exhibit similar patterns.”

Less synchronization, less wear and tear

The periodic fluctuations in electricity demand are already having an impact on hydroelectric power stations. The brief spikes in demand mean that the turbines slow down momentarily before accelerating back to their original rotational speed. This increases wear and tear. With the expansion of storage technologies, such problems could become even more prevalent. In Ireland, for example, where data centres with large-scale battery storage systems currently account for around a fifth of the country’s electricity demand, the amplitude of the 1-minute signal quadrupled between 2016 and 2021. The solution, however, would be simple: “You would simply have to distribute the checks randomly, rather than always starting them at the same time,” says Witthaut.

Original publication: 'One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems', Nature Energy 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41560-026-02144-0

entry.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
entry.content:
HackerTube

It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org!

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

HackerTube:

Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.

EDIT: A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

entry.title: Bidirectional charging during grid outages
entry.content:
Bidirectional Charging During Grid Outages September 7th, 2026 preparedness, solar, tech

The basic problem is that while several manufacturers support having the car power your house when the grid is down ("V2H"), they generally treat it as a separate discharging-only mode. For example, the GM V2H Bundle documentation says "During a power outage, the GM Energy Home Hub safely disconnects your home from the local power grid and enables backup power to flow from the GM Energy Inverter throughout your home" and "Once power is restored, your GM EV will automatically end the discharge session and begin charging" without any mention of recharging the car when the grid is down.

For Fords, automatically powering your house during a grid outage was a big selling point in the F150 Lightning marketing campaign, but they now say "The Ford Charge Station Pro, required for Automatic Home Backup Power, is no longer for sale", probably because the F150 Lightning has been discontinued. And it looks to me like even then they didn't support bidirectional charging during a grid outage. The only option today is V2H via a transfer switch, which doesn't let you charge an F150.

For Kia, there's Wallbox's Quasar 2. Unfortunately this is a mess where Wallbox is very enthusiastic and says V2H works, but then customers run into trouble actually trying to use it. And it doesn't work with current models, plus "Solar Charging cannot be used simultaneously with ... V2H".

The only way I can see to do this today is with Tesla Powershare + Cybertruck, which says "If the system includes a UL 1741-listed solar system and there is capacity in the backup panel, ensure the solar system is included in the backup circuit to allow Cybertruck to recharge during an outage." But I don't want a Cybertruck, and (counting the cost of a Cybertruck over a vehicle we'd normally buy) this would be way more expensive than the Enphase 10C I'm considering installing.

Another possibility is that Enphase is planning on shipping a bidirectional EV charger, but I don't see anything more recent than a 2026-02-02 announcement that they're "targeting volume production beginning in Q4 2026" and they say "projected vehicle compatibility and bidirectional functionality will depend on automaker enablement, vehicle software, applicable standards, and final product specifications." I suspect it will slip into 2027, MA availability will be even later, and when it does come out I'd need to buy a specific new EV (expensive).

I don't want to wait that long to get good backup power in place, since I want to be prepared for a world that might change quickly in the next few years. So I'll probably go ahead with the smaller emergencies-only battery.

[1] All of this assumes we have an electric car. Which we don't, but our shared Honda Fit is a 2013 and while it's been a fantastic car I don't expect it to last that much longer. A plug-in hybrid or full EV are possibilities for a next car. I think our families are unusually poorly suited for full EVs since we don't use the car much (minimal gas savings and pollution reduction) and a larger than typical proportion of our trips are long (ex: driving to play a dance).

entry.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
entry.content:
An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems

Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them.

To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books.

For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile.

“I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient, he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today?

Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says.

Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible

In 2 Kings 4:42-44, Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.

In 1 Kings 17:8-16, Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.

In Judges 7:9-15, a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.

In 2 Kings 4:38-41, during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.

Grossi discovered it had other advantages: It was hardier and more self-sufficient than commercial varieties. It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. Indeed, it seemed so superior to its industrial cousins that he thought of it no longer as a freak of nature but as a wonder. He dubbed it grano del miracolo—“miracle grain” or “miracle wheat.”

Grossi’s discovery came at just the right time. In Italy in the 1990s, a burgeoning slow-food movement aimed to preserve traditional farming practices and promote natural diets.

Grossi hoped that miracolo could ride this slow-food wave, becoming both a portal to the past and a passage to a future. Perhaps, he thought, miracolo could help other farmers bring back ancient grains, leading the movement that is changing how we make bread, a staple of the human diet. And today, as climate change makes droughts, heat waves and plant disease outbreaks more frequent and intense, a grain that has shown it can fend for itself would help keep that bread on the table.

Farmers began cultivating wheat about 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent—the area of the Middle East known as the Cradle of Civilization. Thousands of years ago, the hardy and adaptable plant took hold in Europe and Asia. Compared with our modern crops, these ancient wheats were much taller, outperforming other grasses in the field.

Over the millennia, humans bred different varieties of wheat, some yielding less grain and others more. As human populations grew, the strains of wheat that brought plentiful harvests became more desirable. That pattern accelerated amid the upheavals of the early 20th century. By the early 1920s, Italy was still recovering from World War I and unable to grow enough grain to sustain itself; the country was importing roughly a third of its wheat. When fascist leader Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922, he launched a campaign to “free the Italian people from the slavery of foreign bread,” by pushing for wheat varieties that yielded greater harvests. The Italian government promoted and planted these “elite” varieties, then distributed the seeds to farmers. Named la Battaglia del Grano, or the Battle of Wheat, this campaign became a global model for agrarian development.

In the United States, wheat harvests were then still plentiful, but not for long: By the early 1930s, amid unprecedented droughts, American farmers found the land was exhausted. The result was the Dust Bowl, during which the previously fertile soils of the Great Plains turned into a desert. American farmers had to look for more drought-resistant varieties that still yielded enough grain.

The midcentury Green Revolution, a movement launched by the American agronomist Norman Borlaug, focused on selective breeding and boosted crop production. This work spread worldwide, feeding countless people. The wheat that was created was indeed more plentiful, yet it came with trade-offs. The petite plants couldn’t always outcompete weeds and were susceptible to disease, so growers used weed killers, fungicides and fertilizer to sustain the crops. Little did they know that these practices would only weaken the health of the soil—while making the wheat even less resilient to changing climate and extreme weather events.

In the 1990s, Grossi sensed that anxiety over wheat harvests was building. That’s why, after he grew wheat from those seeds in the attic, he set out to put the hardy ancient grain back on the table. First, he realized he’d have to solve a big problem: Bread made from the wheat leavened poorly, rising only to fall again. In the early 2000s, he began discussing this challenge with an old local baker who shunned modern machines and still kneaded his dough by hand. The baker was intrigued. The two men started experimenting.

They tried letting the dough rise in smaller batches, using wicker baskets that were taller and helped the dough keep its shape. Soon, the two found another secret: Less kneading made miracolo leaven even better. “The dough was rising, and it was holding its shape,” Grossi says.

One new fan of the bread was Beniamino Perobelli, a student in food science at the University of Parma, who tasted the miracolo bread at a local farmers market and dedicated his undergraduate thesis to investigating its nutritional value. That work bore out what Grossi had already intuited: This wheat was truly ancient—and truly special.

Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali, then a professor at the University of Parma, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum—literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains.

The food scientists found that, compared with modern wheats, grano del miracolo was richer in phosphorus and iron. Moreover, to their surprise, they found that T. turgidum had less gluten than modern wheat. And it packed a lot of lysine and tryptophan, the essential amino acids that serve as proteins’ building blocks. It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow. “The richness of microelements, minerals, and the greater presence of proteins other than gluten were very pleasant surprises,” says Perobelli, now a corporate social responsibility and sustainability manager with Rigoni di Asiago, an Italian company that produces organic fruit spreads, honey and more.

For Grossi, Perobelli’s findings offered scientific proof of his grain’s goodness. He persuaded Molino Grassi, a local organic grain company, to offer the flour to artisanal bakers. Over the next few years, Grossi upped production, so Molino Grassi could sell the flour to restaurants and consumers in Italy and abroad.

By the 2010s, traditional recipes were enjoying a renaissance. So were artisanal bakers and pasta makers, who also became more discerning about which grains they used, says Francesco Sottile, an expert in biodiversity of agrosystems at the University of Palermo.

Ancient grains aren’t necessarily perfect. For example, Grossi has found that miracolo’s height can be a liability—which may be why it fell out of favor with Mussolini. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests. But Grossi circumvented the problem by planting miracolo with shorter wheat varieties that provide structural support. “I’m quite happy because I developed something that’s like a discovery,” he says.

Relying on a limited number of wheat cultivars, Sottile argues, leaves humanity vulnerable to agricultural disasters: prolonged droughts, extreme heat, new diseases or pests that develop resistance to our chemicals. Diversifying grains reduces the risk—even if some varieties succumb to environmental pressures, others will stand.

Sottile shared an example. “I’m based in Sicily,” he says, where 2024 saw “one of the worst droughts in the last 35 to 40 years.” It was so bad that many commercial wheat growers abandoned their fields in April of that year, realizing they wouldn’t be able to reap the seeds they sowed. Sottile was heartened to see a better fate among smaller-batch farmers who grew heritage grains, more resilient to extreme weather.

“Most of the farmers who were adopting ancient grains, they were able to collect, to harvest,” Sottile says. The world needs more crop biodiversity, he adds—including more ancient grains like grano del miracolo. By the same token, we need more people like Grossi, who, much like the ancient grain he sows, have the tenacity to make a miracle happen.

Stories of gods and grains

“Miracle wheat” is hardly the first divine cereal. Across millennia, gods have taught mortals how to earn their bread

By Sonja Anderson

Greece: While Dionysus provided grapes and Athena was responsible for olives, the goddess Demeter brought grain to the Greeks. In myth, the latter goddess taught farming to a man named Triptolemus (pictured at right), then sent him out on a winged chariot to deliver the knowledge to all of Greece—an episode immortalized on ancient vases.

Mesopotamia: Ancient Sumerians of the Fertile Crescent attributed farming to Ashnan, the grain goddess, “whose face is honey-covered / The lady, the procreatress, the vigor of the land,” per an ancient Sumerian poem. In myth, Ashnan and her sibling Lahar, deity of livestock, once drunkenly debated whether grains or sheep were more important. Enlil and Enki, the paramount Sumerian gods, declared Ashnan the winner, saying that without grain—often fed to herds—there could be no sheep.

Egypt: Osiris ruled over death and the afterlife but was also a god of fertility, and it was said he taught mankind to cultivate wheat. Ancient Egyptians became famously adept at managing this crop: Their growing seasons regularly produced surpluses, thanks to the Nile’s floods. Some priests honored Osiris by planting grain in earthenware shaped like the god.

China: Some ancient Chinese myths trace the country’s agriculture back to one emperor of legend: Shennong, born of a princess and a dragon some 4,000 years ago. The ruler supposedly had a bull’s head and a man’s body and is known as the divine farmer, or emperor of five grains (including rice, millets and wheat). He taught his people how to till their land, expanding the ancient Chinese diet—consisting mainly of meat, clams and wild fruits—to include grains and vegetables.

Mexico: Quetzalcoatl was a deity of the Aztec civilization who, according to myth, created the humans of our current era—the Fifth Sun—and their world. He taught people how to carve rocks, dye cotton, read the stars and—most important—grow food. One day, Quetzalcoatl observed a black ant carrying a kernel of corn, turned himself into an ant and followed the insect through a crack in a stone mountain, where he found a trove of maize, beans, peppers and sage. He took a corn kernel, brought it to man and taught him how to plant it.

entry.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
entry.content:
The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks

One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users (DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade”, Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture, and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway).

For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX. In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. (Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.)

But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?”

Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward:

Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised) Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.) Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating) Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse

The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.:

I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test.

To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite.

Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs, etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required.

One thing I learned from this experiment is that everything I’m measuring is very stochastic. LLMs are random-word generators, so sometimes you get a low dice-roll and an agent goes off on some weird tangent wasting a bunch of tokens, through no fault of the framework or its tools. Lighthouse itself can give inconsistent results as well: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) may decide that one image is the “largest” element, then pick another one on the next run. It’s hard to have a perfectly fair experiment, but running multiple iterations did help, and I’ve tried to be honest about the variance.

With all that throat-clearing out of the way, let’s get to the results.

Results

I’m going to break this down by multiple dimensions: cost to build, quality, and maintainability. For each framework/meta-framework, I took the median of 5 runs: in other words, I built the same app 5 times in the same framework. (Yes, this is the kind of zany thing you can do with coding agents these days.)

The exception was Angular, which failed to create a measurable app twice, so I took 3 iterations instead for some metrics. (This is explained below.)

Cost Cost per run, in US dollars Framework Hono+htmx $2.67 Astro $2.76 Nuxt $2.82 Vanilla $2.98 Next.js $3.14 Qwik $3.27 TanStack Start $3.54 SolidStart $3.79 React Router $3.81 SvelteKit $4.28 Gracile+Lit $4.65 Angular $4.97 02468

Note that this quotes the API prices directly from Claude Code and doesn’t actually represent how much money I spent. I’m on a Max plan, so this was just part of my overall $100/month.

Note also the variance: React Router’s median is roughly $1 worse than that of Hono+htmx, but the cheapest version of React Router ($2.82) is still cheaper than the most expensive version of Hono+htmx ($3.19). However some reliable patterns do emerge.

Most clearly, SvelteKit, Gracile+Lit, and Angular are more expensive to build than the other frameworks. For SvelteKit, this may be due to the fact that the agents read the SvelteKit v3 migration guide in every run, likely because it’s too new to be in Opus 5.5’s training data. Similarly for Gracile, the agents didn’t know the framework very well and either cloned the Gracile repo or read its compiled source from node_modules. For Angular it seems to be a function of the total code size (see below).

I should also mention that not every agent made use of an MCP/skill/Claude Code plugin, nor did every framework have one:

Click to see AI tool usage Framework Installed Used by the agents? Angular Angular MCP and Angular agent skills MCP in 3/5 runs, skill tool in 4/5 runs, skill files in 2/5 Astro Astro MCP server MCP in 2/5 runs Gracile+Lit N/A N/A Hono+htmx Hono skills Skill tool in 5/5 runs Next.js next-devtools-mcp and next-dev-loop skill Skill files in 1/5 runs, AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs Nuxt Nuxt MCP N/A Qwik N/A N/A React Router React Router skill Skill tool in 5/5 runs, skill files in 5/5 runs SolidStart N/A N/A SvelteKit Svelte Claude Code plugin MCP in 5/5 runs TanStack Start N/A Skill files in 2/5 runs Vanilla N/A N/A

For example, TanStack Start’s agent only discovered its skill files in 2/5 runs (they’re shipped in the node_modules of the project). For Nuxt, the MCP was never used by the agents. For Next.js, agents only read the skill file in 1/5 runs and the AGENTS.md in 2/5 runs. This is a wide range of results, which points back to the stochastic nature of LLMs. I still consider this a valid experiment, though, because I doubt many vibe-coders are shouting at their agents in all-caps to use the MCP (and plenty are probably skipping it entirely).

Also, if you’re wondering how I came up with Hono+htmx: essentially, I wanted htmx represented somehow, and Hono seemed like a fine pairing (i.e. as a JavaScript alternative to Rails/Django/etc.). As for Gracile+Lit, I wanted web components represented via their standard-bearer framework (Lit), and was only aware of Gracile as a meta-framework. If there are better candidates, then those would be great for a follow-up experiment.

For “Vanilla,” note that the agent was told to use “vanilla JavaScript or TypeScript with Vite, without a UI framework.” Surprisingly, this underperforms several frameworks, which seems to demonstrate that having some framework can be better than nothing (or better than raw Vite, anyway). Vite was chosen because it undergirds many frameworks and represents fairly standard and agnostic JavaScript infrastructure.

The total time and tokens track pretty closely with the cost:

Time per run Framework Astro 8.2 Hono+htmx 8.6 Nuxt 9.0 Vanilla 10.1 TanStack Start 10.3 Qwik 10.7 SvelteKit 10.8 Next.js 10.9 SolidStart 11.2 Gracile+Lit 12.1 React Router 12.5 Angular 17.2 0510152025
Tokens per run, in millions Framework Nuxt 3.85 Astro 4.13 Hono+htmx 4.26 Next.js 4.99 Vanilla 5.00 Qwik 5.64 TanStack Start 7.07 SolidStart 7.13 React Router 7.58 SvelteKit 8.53 Gracile+Lit 9.04 Angular 9.76 051015

The tokens, by the way, were reported by Claude Code. The duration is just the total wall-clock time.

Quality

Of course, because I think that outcomes matter, I also tested the agents with Lighthouse. As software developers, I think it’s important that we not only build things cheaply but also performantly and accessibly.

I should first note two caveats about my benchmark:

The Pokémon app is small and doesn’t represent a large, complex real-world application. Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals in general are biased against SPAs, so the MPA frameworks are almost guaranteed to win on metrics like Total Blocking Time (TBT), JavaScript bytes, etc. I considered adding some in-app performance metrics but backed off because it added complexity and variability to the benchmark, and these would be metrics I invented as opposed to industry standards.

For simplicity’s sake, I’m only reporting the scores for the home page. There are other pages, but they all score fairly similarly or they have wild swings in metrics like LCP, so it just complicates things to include them.

In short: the Lighthouse scores for Performance, Accessibility, and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) are nearly saturated and don’t vary much by framework:

Framework CLS Performance Accessibility Angular 0.000 98 100 Astro 0.000 100 100 Gracile+Lit 0.000 100 100 Hono+htmx 0.000 100 100 Next.js 0.000 99 100 Nuxt 0.000 100 100 Qwik 0.000 100 100 React Router 0.000 100 100 SolidStart 0.000 100 100 SvelteKit 0.000 100 100 TanStack Start 0.000 99 100 Vanilla 0.111 97 100

So to get some more interesting numbers, we need to look at other metrics. The most reliable one is the JavaScript bytes sent, which largely tracks the client-side framework size:

JavaScript bytes transferred Framework Astro 0 Vanilla 7 Gracile+Lit 8 Hono+htmx 18 SvelteKit 36 SolidStart 40 Qwik 40 Nuxt 84 Angular 93 React Router 115 TanStack Start 118 Next.js 142 050100150

The Total Blocking Time (TBT) is interesting in that it’s not purely a function of the JavaScript bytes; some of the apps spend more time on the main thread than others. That said, the numbers are all quite small:

Total Blocking Time (TBT) Framework Astro 0 Gracile+Lit 0 Hono+htmx 0 SvelteKit 0 Vanilla 0 TanStack Start 1 Qwik 3 SolidStart 11 React Router 17 Nuxt 40 Next.js 71 Angular 103 0255075100125

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is highly variable due to the aforementioned issues with the metric itself. As expected, though, it does broadly punish SPAs and reward MPAs:

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) Framework Astro 810 Gracile+Lit 956 Hono+htmx 978 Qwik 979 SvelteKit 1130 SolidStart 1204 Vanilla 1667 Nuxt 1727 React Router 1729 Angular 1954 TanStack Start 2028 Next.js 2090 05001000150020002500

Note that the wild variance in the Next.js numbers can be explained by the fact that one app avoided lazy-loading images and the other four didn’t. Astro and Vanilla have similar swings that appear to be caused by prioritization or LCP quirks.

In general though, it’s unsurprising that the metric tends to reward MPAs that paint quickly with HTML rather than SPAs that paint after client-side JavaScript runs (along with possibly multiple throttled round-trips to grab the Pokémon data). Ignoring variance, LCP here is mostly a function of JavaScript bundle size. (Qwik is a notable exception here: technically it’s an SPA that uses client-side routing, but it scores among the MPA frameworks.)

Note though that some of the frameworks varied in whether they focused more on the client or the server, or even whether they used a client-side framework. For example, the Gracile agent didn’t even use Lit in two runs. For “Vanilla,” the agent had full latitude (aside from being told to use Vite), but still chose to build an SPA all 5 times.

SSR vs CSR is also partly where the trouble with Angular came from: in 2 runs, the agent built an SSR app that rejected non-localhost (even though the instructions explicitly said that the app would be behind a reverse proxy). I considered this a valid failure to adhere to the spec and decided not to re-run the 2 failed iterations. (This only affects the code size and performance measurements; I have reported all 5 Angular iterations for the “cost” section.)

Maintainability

There are lots of ways to measure maintainability (including fancy things like cyclomatic complexity), but I decided to keep it simple and report something tried-and-true: total lines of code.

Lines of code Framework Hono+htmx 1370 Nuxt 1415 Astro 1461 Vanilla 1492 Next.js 1539 React Router 1564 SvelteKit 1611 SolidStart 1630 TanStack Start 1697 Gracile+Lit 1717 Qwik 1744 Angular 2009 05001000150020002500

To me this is one of the more interesting charts. In a sense, the whole point of a framework is to reduce the amount of code you need to maintain. In Rich Harris’s memorable words:

“Frameworks are not tools for organizing your code; they are tools for organizing your mind.”

– Rich Harris, “Rethinking reactivity”

In the agentic era, this hits even harder because the code size ultimately impacts the number of tokens, including in future edits, meaning it affects the literal cost to maintain a codebase over time. This doesn’t mean that succinctness is the only value that matters, but it’s certainly interesting to see that Hono+htmx can do roughly the same thing as Angular with ~70% of the code (and faster, to boot).

Conclusion

There are many ways you could improve this benchmark. For example, you could mandate that the agent use Service Workers for offline caching, or optimize the Pokémon image files, or use lazy-loading, fetchpriority, the Speculation Rules API, etc. Even though I know a lot of these performance hacks, I deliberately didn’t steer the agents toward any of them, because it’s not what a typical vibe-coder would do.

On the other hand, this entire benchmark could be cheated by just pre-generating all the HTML files as static assets (there are only so many Pokémon). I specifically forebade that in the instructions and made it an explicit check in the test harness, because I felt that it wasn’t in the spirit of the benchmark. (My aim is to simulate a large volume of possibly-dynamic data, which is more challenging than a purely static site.)

You could also improve the way I ran the benchmark by running more iterations, using different coding agents, trying different effort levels, using different frameworks or different versions of the frameworks, trying with and without MCPs/skills, testing in more browsers than just Chromium, building different types of apps, etc. I didn’t do these things mostly in the interest of time. However, if anybody wants to run the benchmark themselves or fork it, it’s on GitHub, so I encourage you to go nuts. I’ll happily report your results here (along with any mistakes or flaws you may find).

My goal here is not to write the end-all-be-all benchmark for “I’m a vibe-coder, which framework should I choose?” The point of this post is to demonstrate that it’s possible in the era of AI coding to still make decisions based on evidence rather than vibes. The benchmark itself is largely vibe-coded, although I did review the code, so if there are mistakes then please consider them mine. I’d also be perfectly happy to see competitor frameworks try to improve on what I’ve done here.

I’m also not trying to vilify any particular framework. I didn’t know which one would “win” before running the benchmark, although I did suspect that MPAs would outperform SPAs (which I’ve cheerfully admitted throughout this post). You could certainly write a more SPA-favored benchmark by making the app a complex dashboard, a video game, a productivity app, etc. You could also pick different metrics: Lighthouse and the Core Web Vitals are pretty tough on SPAs, so you could measure in-app interactivity instead.

I’m also sure that the framework authors themselves could improve their frameworks or AI tools and do better on this benchmark. I have a strong suspicion, for example, that the current crop of MCPs and skills may be doing more harm than good. So if this post is the last word on these frameworks’ performance, I’ll be sorely disappointed. I’m sure there are also emerging frameworks that are champing at the bit to do well on benchmarks such as this one.

If nothing else, I hope this post inspires you to apply additional scrutiny to your choice of JavaScript framework in this weird new era of vibe coding. Are you really picking your tech stack based on evidence? Or are you just going with what you already know? That’s certainly understandable, especially if you’re still reading, reviewing, and debugging the code yourself. But if you’ve gone largely hands-free, then what attachment do you really have to the choices you made back when you were typing code line-by-line like an animal? If you’re re-evaluating the entire way you build software, maybe it’s worth re-evaluating what you type after npm install? Just saying.

Personally, I don’t have any attachment to the frameworks I’ve evaluated above, except that I believe we should strive to build the best possible experiences for our users. I know and respect many of the authors of the above frameworks, and I know that they are working tirelessly for the same values I champion. My hope is just to push the entire community in a better direction toward better, faster, and more accessible frameworks to power the next generation of web apps.

Addendum

Framework versions used in the test (note Qwik had a patch release partway through the test):

Framework Version Angular @angular/core 22.2.3 Astro astro 7.4.2 Gracile+Lit @gracile/gracile 0.11.0, lit 3.3.3 Hono+htmx hono 4.13.14, htmx.org 2.0.11 Next.js next 16.4.3, react 19.3.1 Nuxt nuxt 4.6.2, vue 3.5.44 Qwik @builder.io/qwik-city 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5), @builder.io/qwik 1.20.2 (iteration 1), 1.20.3 (iterations 2, 3, 4, 5) React Router react-router 8.5.0, react 19.3.1 SolidStart @solidjs/start 2.1.0, solid-js 1.9.17 SvelteKit @sveltejs/kit 3.1.0, svelte 5.57.2 TanStack Start @tanstack/react-start 1.169.4, react 19.3.1 Vanilla vite 8.3.5

entry.title: Domain hacks with unusual Unicode characters (2018)
entry.content:
Unicode contains a range of symbols which don't get much use. For example, there are separate symbols for TradeMark - ™, Service Mark - ℠, and Prescriptions - ℞.

Nestling among the "Letterlike Symbols" are two curious entries. Both of these are single characters:

Telephone symbol - ℡ Numero Sign - №

What's interesting is both .tel and .no are Top-Level-Domains (TLD) on the Domain Name System (DNS).

So my contact site - https://edent.tel/ - can be written as - https://edent.℡/

And the Norwegian domain name registry NORID can be accessed at https://www.norid.№/

Copy and paste those links - they work in any browser!

Is this limited to TLDs?

No! This works ANYWHERE in a domain name. Copy and paste these examples:

Script https://ℰ𝒳𝒜ℳ𝓟ℒℰ.𝒞𝓞ℳ/ Math Bold https://𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞.𝐜𝐨𝐦/ Fraktur https://𝖊𝖝𝖆𝖒𝖕𝖑𝖊.𝖈𝖔𝖒/ Math bold italic https://𝒆𝒙𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆.𝒄𝒐𝒎/ Math bold script https://𝓮𝔁𝓪𝓶𝓹𝓵𝓮.𝓬𝓸𝓶/ Double struck https://𝕖𝕩𝕒𝕞𝕡𝕝𝕖.𝕔𝕠𝕞/ Monospace https://𝚎𝚡𝚊𝚖𝚙𝚕𝚎.𝚌𝚘𝚖/ Super script https://ᵉˣᵃᵐᵖˡᵉ.ᶜᵒᵐ/ Sub script https://ₑₓₐₘₚₗₑ.cₒₘ/ NB not all characters supported Math sans bold https://𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺/ Math sans bold italic https://𝙚𝙭𝙖𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚.𝙘𝙤𝙢/ Math sans italic https://𝘦𝘹𝘢𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘦.𝘤𝘰𝘮/ Math Squared https://🄴🅇🄰🄼🄿🄻🄴.🄲🄾🄼/ NB the dot must not be squared Circled https://ⓔⓧⓐⓜⓟⓛⓔ.ⓒⓞⓜ/ NB the dot must not be circled

There are a whole bunch more miscellaneous characters you can use:

 How does this work?

Magic! Which is to say, I think it is the browser doing the conversion. DNS Servers don't successfully reply to queries about .℡ domains.

The browser sees the .℡ and then follows the IDNA2008 process listed in RFC5895 to normalise it:

map characters to the "Simple_Lowercase_Mapping" property (the fourteenth column) in <http://www.unicode.org/Public/UNIDATA/UnicodeData.txt>, if any.

The ℡ entry is:

2121;TELEPHONE SIGN;So;0;ON;<compat> 0054 0045 004C;;;;N;T E L SYMBOL;;;;

U+0054 is T, U+0045 is E, U+004C is L.

You can test this in Python using:

python -c 'import sys;print sys.argv[1].decode("utf-8").encode("idna")' "℡" Does this work?

Yes! I asked people on Twitter whether they could access my website using a .℡ - and it appeared to work on every modern browser and operating system.

It even works on command line tools like wget and curl.

It does fail in some circumstances:

 What are the limitations?

Two main ones:

Sites like Twitter and Facebook don't recognise it as a valid URl and refuse to auto link it. Some command line tools like dig and host don't understand it Bashdig edent.℡ ; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> edent.℡ ;; global options: +cmd ;; Got answer: ;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 55282 Is this useful?

Obviously yes. This may be the most important discovery of the decade. You get cool looking URls and get to save a couple of characters on specific domains, at the minor expense of working inconsistently.

It could also be used for evading URl filters.

Every modern browser supports these "fancy" domain names - but most websites won't automatically link to them. So sharing on Facebook doesn't work.

Where can it be used?

Here are the single characters which can be normalised down to a valid TLD. They're mostly country codes, but there are a few interesting exceptions:

㏕ - US Military ℡ - .tel registry № - Norway ㍳ - Australia ㍷ - Dominica ㎀ - Panama ㎁ - Namibia ㎃ - Morocco ㎊ - French Polynesia ㎋ - Norfolk Island ㎏ - Kyrgyzstan ㎖ - Mali ㎙ - Federated States of Micronesia ﬁ - Finland ㎜ - Myanmar ㎝ - Cameroon ㎞ & ㏎ - Comoros ㎰ - Palestine ㎳ - Montserrat ㎷ & ㎹ - Republic of Maldives. ㎺ - Palau ㎽ & ㎿ - Malawi ㏄ - Cocos (Keeling) Islands ㏅ - Democratic Republic of Congo ㏉ - Guyana ㏗ - Philippines ㏘ - Saint Pierre and Miquelon ㏚ - Puerto Rico ㏛ - Suriname ㏜ - El Salvador ℠ - San Marino ™ - Turkmenistan ﬆ & ﬅ - São Tomé and Príncipe ㎇ - Great Britain ( Obsolete) ß - South Sudan ( Not available) ㏌ - India and Indiana (subdomain of .us) Ⅵ & ⅵ - Virgin Islands and Virginia (subdomain of .us) ﬂ - Florida (subdomain of .us) ㎚ - New Mexico (subdomain of .us) ㎵ - Nevada (subdomain of .us) ㍵ - As part of .ovh

If you can find any more, please stick a comment in the box below.

You can always reach this blog post at:

https://🅂𝖍𝐤ₛᵖ𝒓.ⓜ𝕠𝒃𝓲/🆆🆃🅵/

entry.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
entry.content:
Fast, robust, accurate content-aware diffing.

Robust: can diff 99.95% of code changes Content-aware: 98.8% of changes diffed using content-specific algorithms Content Fast: under 100ms Accurate: perfect Accurate: near-perfect Code 98% 70% 92% Pictures 96% 69% 91% Cursors 100% 85% 100% Fonts 95% 82% 100% Archives 88% 87% 87% Message catalogs 100% 83% 83% PDFs 57% 100% 100%

Speed measured on a T14s, Intel Core i7-1370P with 32 GB RAM (see Fast). PDFs have fewer than ten judged test cases (see Accurate).

See it in the browser: twenty real code changes, recorded from the command-line tool and compared side by side in Unix diff and in OmniDiff, and content examples: an OpenDocument file, a compiled translation catalog, and pictures, still and animated.

Various light and dark themes are available:

Files are diffed based on type. A PDF diagram with one box renamed, and a web font with twenty icons redrawn:

cargo install --locked omnidiff

This command builds OmniDiff from source, with the dependency versions it was tested with. You need a C compiler on PATH and a Rust toolchain, rustc 1.92 or later. The build compiles every tree-sitter grammar from C. The first cargo install takes a few minutes, because of this and the lto = "fat" release profile.

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon), and Windows are attached to every GitHub release.

macOS and Linux:

brew install ivankovic/omnidiff/omnidiff

.deb packages for amd64 and arm64 are available in a signed apt repository:

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://ivankovic.github.io/omnidiff/apt/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg > /dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/omnidiff-archive-keyring.gpg] \ https://ivankovic.github.io/omnidiff/apt stable main" \ | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/omnidiff.list > /dev/null sudo apt update && sudo apt install omnidiff

On NixOS, or anywhere with Nix installed:

nix run github:ivankovic/omnidiff

If flakes are not enabled in your Nix configuration, add --extra-experimental-features 'nix-command flakes' after nix.

Recipes for Arch and Gentoo live in packaging/: the PKGBUILD builds locally with makepkg -si, and the Gentoo ebuild is ready for an overlay. The two distros are overwhelmed and their repositories open and close to new packages sporadically.

VS Code does not yet let an extension replace its built-in diff view. The API is implemented upstream but unreleased; the extension will adopt it when it ships.

VS Code - omnidiff-vscode. Search for OmniDiff in the Extensions view, or code --install-extension ivankovic.omnidiff. Also on Open VSX for VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf. Neovim - omnidiff.nvim. omnidiff # open an empty viewer; press o to pick each file omnidiff BEFORE AFTER # open directly into the diff of two files

Press ? in the viewer for the full list of keybindings.

The TUI uses 24-bit color when the terminal advertises it with COLORTERM=truecolor, and the nearest 256 colors otherwise (macOS Terminal.app, or most terminals over ssh, which does not forward COLORTERM). If your terminal supports 24-bit color but does not advertise it, run export COLORTERM=truecolor.

For reviewing changes in a browser, see codereview.

Note: codereview is at v0.0.0; use it at your own risk.

omnidiff --headless BEFORE AFTER, or its synonym --batch, prints the diff as plain text, with optional color, instead of opening the TUI. Use this for scripts or CI. Headless mode also starts automatically whenever stdout is not a terminal, for example when piped into less or redirected to a file. Because of this, omnidiff BEFORE AFTER | less works without the flag.

OmniDiff collapses long runs of unchanged lines. It keeps 3 lines of context on each side of a change (override with --context N), the same convention as diff -u. OmniDiff also prefixes each hunk with the nearest enclosing function, class, or struct line, when that line is not otherwise visible. This shows the location of a change deep inside a large file.

Colors are on by default; pass --color never, or set NO_COLOR=1, to disable ANSI colors, for example when you redirect output to a file - --color always forces them even under NO_COLOR.

OmniDiff exits 0 on success and 2 on error. For scripting, pass --exit-code to additionally get 1 when the files differ. This follows the diff(1) convention. --exit-code is opt-in rather than the default for the same reason git diff exits 0 even when files differ: OmniDiff's usual non-interactive callers are version control systems driving it as a display tool, and they read a non-zero exit as "the tool failed" - jj warns on every file, and git difftool with difftool.trustExitCode=true aborts the whole diff. (The 7-argument GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF form stays at 0 even with --exit-code, since git treats a non-zero exit there as fatal.)

omnidiff --mode json BEFORE AFTER prints the diff as one JSON object. Its fields are described in src/tui/json_output.schema.json, a JSON Schema.

OmniDiff is a git difftool backend. Run the interactive setup wizard, which asks whether to configure it globally or for the current repository only:

omnidiff git configure git config difftool.omnidiff.cmd 'omnidiff "$LOCAL" "$REMOTE"' git difftool --tool=omnidiff

Run git config diff.tool omnidiff to make plain git difftool use OmniDiff by default, without needing --tool. If you do not want git to ask "view diff ... [Y/n]?" before every file, run git config difftool.prompt false.

git difftool opens the interactive TUI. git diff and git log -p never do. git diff pipes its output through git's pager, and a full-screen TUI cannot draw onto a pipe, so OmniDiff always falls back to plain text there regardless of terminal or GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF config (see "Headless / batch mode" above). If you want the interactive viewer from git, use git difftool, not git diff. If git difftool still doesn't open interactively over SSH, reconnect with ssh -t — the session needs an allocated pseudo-terminal; tmux panes always have one.

OmniDiff also works directly with git diff and git log -p, through GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF. This path needs no difftool config:

GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=omnidiff git diff

Pictures, archives, fonts and the rest of the supported content get a short report of what changed in them. Any other binary file gets a one-line Binary file <path> differs notice instead of a diff, the same stand-in git and diff(1) print for them. Neither ever blocks the rest of a git diff: an external diff that exits non-zero makes git abandon the entire run, so OmniDiff reports an unshowable file as a successful diff of nothing rather than as a failure.

jj does not read git's difftool/diff.external settings, even in a colocated repo, so it needs its own configuration. Run the setup wizard:

omnidiff jj configure jj config set --user merge-tools.omnidiff.program omnidiff jj config set --user merge-tools.omnidiff.diff-args '["$left","$right"]' jj config set --user merge-tools.omnidiff.diff-invocation-mode file-by-file

That registers jj diff --tool omnidiff. To make it the default for plain jj diff as well:

jj config set --user ui.diff-formatter omnidiff

Use --repo in place of --user to configure the current repository only.

diff-invocation-mode = "file-by-file" is required. jj's default hands a diff tool two directory trees; OmniDiff diffs two files, so without this setting every invocation fails. With it, jj passes one changed file pair at a time, keeping each file's real path and extension, so language detection works exactly as it does under git.

jj diff runs its formatter under a pager, so OmniDiff renders in its non-interactive text mode there - the same output git diff gets. jj has no equivalent of git difftool's interactive per-file viewer (its terminal-attached hook, ui.diff-editor, is for jj diffedit/jj split, which edit the right-hand side and read it back - not something a read-only viewer should claim to do), so for the full-screen TUI on a jj repo, run omnidiff BEFORE AFTER directly.

The language is detected from the file extension. A file with an unknown extension is diffed as plain text, line by line, so nothing is refused.

25 languages are parsed with a tree-sitter grammar and diffed structurally:

Language File extensions C .c, .h C# .cs C++ .cc, .cpp, .cxx, .hpp, .hh, .hxx CSS .css, .scss Go .go HTML .html, .htm Java .java JavaScript .js, .mjs, .cjs, .jsx JSON .json Kotlin .kt Lua .lua Perl .pl, .pm PHP .php Python .py, .pyi, .pyw R .r Ruby .rb Rust .rs Scala .scala Shell (Bash) .bash, .sh Swift .swift TSX .tsx TypeScript .ts, .mts, .cts Vimscript .vim XML .xml, .xht, .xhtml, .svg, .glif, .plist, .ui, .qrc, .glade, .xib, .storyboard, .xaml, .vcxproj, .filters, .csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj, .props, .targets, .nuspec, .resx, .wxs, .iml, .manifest, .config, .policy, .xsd, .xsl, .xslt, .xlf, .xliff, .kml, .gpx, .rss, .atom, .graphml, .dae YAML .yaml, .yml

Recognised by extension but diffed as plain text, since no grammar is compiled in: Bazel (.bazel), Dart (.dart), Emacs Lisp (.el), Markdown (.md, .markdown), Protocol Buffers (.proto), SQL (.sql).

Files that are not text are recognised by their bytes, never by their names, and diffed by what they hold:

Content Formats Diffed Pictures PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, ICO, TIFF pixel by pixel, as the eye compares them: how much changed and where; animations frame by frame Archives zip (and so jar, Office documents, EPUB), tar, gzip, xz, bzip2 file by file, each by what it is, archives inside archives included; Java class files as a listing of their fields and methods Fonts TrueType, OpenType, WOFF, WOFF2, EOT glyph by glyph, each drawn, and the font's names and metrics Cursors Windows .cur and .ani, X cursors, Hyprland .hlc size by size and frame by frame Message catalogs gettext .mo, Qt .qm message by message Documents page by page, each page drawn Text in other encodings UTF-16 and UTF-32 with a byte order mark as text, like any other file

Only the members that changed are opened, so a font with two edited glyphs shows two glyphs. Each change is also named by how much of it a reader would see: invisible (only the bytes differ), imperceptible, artifacts (what compression or resampling leaves behind), edited, redrawn or replaced - for text, whitespace, formatting and rewritten stand in for the second, third and fifth.

The TUI shows pictures as pictures: in the terminal's own graphics where it speaks the kitty, sixel or iTerm2 protocol, and in Unicode half blocks everywhere else. b switches to half blocks and back, and OMNIDIFF_GRAPHICS=halfblocks (or kitty, sixel, iterm2) overrides the detection; inside tmux, the terminal in front of the pane decides. An archive, a font or any other container lists its changed members beside the one selected, g shows every changed glyph or picture at once, and Enter opens a text member in the full diff view.

Anything else binary gets the one-line Binary file <path> differs notice.

Copyright (C) 2026 Marko Ivankovic

This program is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of the GNU Affero General Public License as published by the Free Software Foundation, version 3 of the License.

See the LICENSE file for the full text of the License.

A commercial license is available as a monthly subscription through GitHub Sponsors. It covers internal use of omnidiff by your organisation without the source-disclosure obligations of the AGPL. The terms are in LICENSE-COMMERCIAL. Pick the tier that names the commercial license as a benefit. For invoicing or other arrangements, contact me at marko@ivankovic.me.

OmniDiff's goal is:

A median diff in 100ms or less. A 99th-percentile diff in 1000ms or less.

Both are met. Over the 2,302 fixtures in src/test/data/diffs/, measured 2026-10-31 on a laptop, an Intel Core i7-1370P (6 performance and 8 efficiency cores, 20 threads) with 32 GB RAM: p50 4.2ms, p90 35.1ms, p99 177ms, slowest 482ms. 100ms is the 97.6th percentile — 55 fixtures take longer than that, and none takes longer than a second.

Times belong to the machine that measured them, so each machine keeps its own (see research/data/machines.csv): the Intel Xeon E3-1275 v5 server that measured the research figures takes about 2.5 times as long per fixture. Runtime is reported, never gated: make check-quality prints this distribution against the machine's own committed baseline on every push, and warns when the runtime is more than twice the baseline's.

Other content is timed over pairs sampled from the same corpus, decoding included - unpacking an archive, drawing a font's glyphs or a PDF's pages - measured 2026-10-17 on the same laptop:

Content Pairs p50 p90 p99 Under 100ms Pictures 230 1.8ms 41ms 526ms 96.1% Cursors 22 0.6ms 1.3ms 15ms 100% Fonts 100 6.4ms 57ms 826ms 95% Archives 100 2.6ms 156ms 1,938ms 88% Message catalogs 81 0.4ms 1.9ms 4.7ms 100% PDFs 100 69ms 310ms 985ms 57%

Archives miss the 99th-percentile goal: the slowest hold thousands of changed members. PDFs meet both goals, but only 57% of them take under 100ms, since a PDF draws every changed page. make benchmark-content measures this and writes research/data/performance/content_speed/<machine>.csv.

OmniDiff's goal is to process 100% of all commits.

The full test dataset holds the git commit history of about 7,500 open-source git repositories, as available on the main branch. This list of repositories comes from the Gentoo Linux distribution. Find it in list_of_repositories.csv.

Measured over every modified code file in the most recent 50 commits of each of those repositories - 442,530 readable before/after pairs in 25 languages, diffed with no size cap under a 120-second budget and a 6 GB memory cap per process - 442,322 (99.95%) completed successfully. 96 pairs ran past the budget and 112 past the memory cap; the latter are twenty files, nineteen of them generated or embedded - tree-sitter parser tables, codegen, minified bundles, a PNG as a C array - and one commit of a 40,000-line single-header C++ library. Given 24 GB and 300 s, 11 of the 28 files that first hit the cap complete. The run, its harness and every pair that did not complete are documented in research/data/performance/PROVENANCE.md.

Beyond code, over every file changed in the same window - 2,018,010 changes in 7,352 repositories, pictures, fonts and archives included - 98.8% are diffed as text or by their content (98.2% counting each repository at most 1,000 times, so that a few giant ones do not decide it; 6,481 repositories entirely). What is left is mostly text in legacy encodings, compiled objects, audio, and EOT fonts compressed with MicroType Express. The census is documented in research/data/corpus_stats/PROVENANCE.md.

OmniDiff must match a human's own reading of a change, measured against the hand-authored ground-truth mappings in src/test/data/diffs/:

90% of test cases with zero mismatched bytes. 99% of test cases with at most 1% of bytes mismatched.

Neither is met yet. 1,419 of the 2,302 fixtures carry a hand-painted ground truth - every byte of both files labelled with what a human says happened to it - and OmniDiff's own highlighting is compared against it byte by byte, under each of its two highlighting presets (--full, which keeps brackets, separators and leading whitespace, and --minimal, which drops them):

preset zero mismatched bytes at most 1% mismatched mismatched bytes, whole corpus --full 851 (60.0%) 1,241 (87.5%) 99,157 of 73.3M (0.14%) --minimal 987 (69.6%) 1,299 (91.5%) 51,740 of 73.3M (0.07%)

The whole-corpus rate is far below 1% because most of each file is unchanged and nobody gets that wrong; the per-test-case numbers are the ones that count, since a reader meets the mistakes one diff at a time. Most of what is left is not in the matching: rendering the human's own node mapping still disagrees with the painting on 91% of the --full bytes and 91% of the --minimal ones, so the highlighting rules own the gap more than the matcher does.

make update-painting-attribution measures this and writes one row per fixture and preset to research/data/quality/painting_attribution.csv, which the table is counted from; make check-painting-attribution fails if any fixture gets worse.

Other content is judged rather than painted: a human names how much each change is (invisible, imperceptible, artifacts, edited, redrawn or replaced, see supported content) and OmniDiff's verdict is compared with theirs. A test case is perfect when every verdict matches, and near-perfect when every one is at most one level off:

Content Judged Perfect Near-perfect Pictures 130 90 (69%) 118 (91%) Cursors 13 11 (85%) 13 (100%) Fonts 11 9 (82%) 11 (100%) Archives 23 20 (87%) 20 (87%) Message catalogs 12 10 (83%) 10 (83%) PDFs 4 4 (100%) 4 (100%)

make benchmark-content counts these too.

This project uses substantial AI assistance, currently Claude Code. Most commits disclose this with a Co-Authored-By trailer and a link to the session that produced them. This project does not hide that fact. This project does not treat AI assistance as a lesser way to write software.

Contributions are not accepted at this time, to keep the development speed high (see CONTRIBUTING.md). When that changes, AI-assisted contributions will be as welcome as any other, disclosed the same way: whoever submits the work is responsible for understanding it and standing behind it.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for the technology overview, code-quality and testing expectations, project structure, and what CI checks on every push and PR. AGENTS.md has additional AI-agent-specific conventions.

entry.title: Proving and improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
entry.content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

[Submitted on 29 Oct 2026]

Title:Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAsView PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations. Submission historyFrom: Randall Balestriero [view email]
